title: How do you prepare training records for a GMP inspection in Australia or the EU?
seoTitle: GMP inspection training: TGA and EU
description: What GMP inspectors check for training under EU GMP Chapter 2 and the PIC/S Guide used by the TGA, how deficiencies are classed, and a checklist.
shortAnswer: To prepare training records for a good manufacturing practice (GMP) inspection by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) or an EU national inspectorate, show approved training programs for everyone whose work can affect quality, records of initial and continuing training, and periodic assessment of training effectiveness, as EU GMP Chapter 2 and the PIC/S GMP Guide require. Inspectors also talk with operators to assess their knowledge, and PIC/S classifies inadequate training or missing training records as a major deficiency example.
keyTakeaways: EU GMP Chapter 2 and Part I of the PIC/S GMP Guide (paragraphs 2.10 to 2.14) require training programs approved by the head of Production or Quality Control, continuing training, periodic assessment of practical effectiveness, and kept records.
The EU inspection procedure tells inspectors to discuss observations with key personnel, supervisors, and operators to assess their knowledge and competence.
PIC/S guidance on classifying deficiencies lists inadequate initial and ongoing training, or no training records, as an example of a major deficiency.
The TGA adopted PIC/S Guide PE009-17 (except Annexes 4, 5, and 14) on 1 September 2025; PE009-18 revises only Annex 19.
Directive (EU) 2017/1572 requires the effectiveness of GMP training to be verified.

sections.heading: Who inspects GMP and against which rules?

blocks.text: In Australia the TGA inspects manufacturers against the manufacturing principles, which adopt the PIC/S Guide to GMP; in the EU, national competent authorities inspect against EudraLex Volume 4, using procedures in the [Compilation of Union Procedures on Inspections](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/compliance-research-development/good-manufacturing-practice/compilation-union-procedures-inspections-exchange-information) maintained by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). The personnel training text is substantively shared, because the PIC/S Guide and EU GMP Part I Chapter 2 use the same paragraph structure.

items: **EU:** [EU GMP Chapter 2](/regulations/eu-gmp-chapter-2-personnel-training-requirements), in operation since 16 February 2014, and Article 7(4) of Directive (EU) 2017/1572, which requires initial and ongoing training whose effectiveness is verified.

**Australia:** the [TGA GMP personnel training requirements](/regulations/tga-gmp-personnel-training-requirements), set through the Therapeutic Goods (Manufacturing Principles) Determination 2020, which adopts PIC/S Guide PE009-17 excluding Annexes 4, 5, and 14 from 1 September 2025.
**Sterile products:** Annex 1 requires gowning qualification with reassessment at least annually; see [EU GMP Annex 1 training](/regulations/eu-gmp-annex-1-sterile-manufacturing-training).
**Active substances:** Part II paragraph 3.12 requires regular training by qualified individuals, with records and periodic assessment.

sections.heading: What do GMP inspectors look at for training?

blocks.text: Inspectors look at personnel as one of the core areas of a general GMP inspection, and they test training both on paper and by talking with the people doing the work. The European Commission's procedure on the [conduct of inspections of pharmaceutical manufacturers or importers](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/regulatory-procedural-guideline/conduct-inspections-pharmaceutical-manufacturers-or-importers_en.pdf) (in force from 1 January 2024) lists personnel among the areas a general GMP inspection will normally examine.

blocks.title: EU procedure, section 4.3
blocks.text: "During the inspection the inspector should always discuss observations as they arise with the key personnel, supervisors and operators in order to establish facts, indicate areas of concern and to assess the knowledge and competence of these personnel."

The same procedure says the company should explain significant changes in facilities, equipment, products, and personnel since the last inspection during the opening meeting, which normally takes no more than 30 minutes. Training records are therefore often requested for new key personnel, new processes, and areas where observations arise.

PIC/S guidance on [data management and integrity](https://picscheme.org/docview/4234) (PI 041-1) adds that personnel should be trained for their specific duties, including good documentation practices, and that there should be evidence of the effectiveness of training on critical procedures, such as electronic data review.
Inspectors test the elements of paragraphs 2.10 to 2.14 of Chapter 2 and the PIC/S Guide Part I. This original table maps each to the record an inspector may ask for.

blocks.text: Deficiencies are commonly classed as critical, major, or other, and PIC/S publishes the [PIC/S Guidance on Classification of GMP Deficiencies](https://picscheme.org/docview/2303) (PI 040-1, in force since 1 January 2019) to support that classification. The guidance aims to make classification consistent across inspectorates and to tell industry how deficiencies are classified, while noting that classification also depends on the context of the finding and the site's quality history.

items: **Critical:** a deficiency that has produced, or leads to a significant risk of producing, a product harmful to the patient, or where fraud, misrepresentation, or falsification of products or data is observed.

**Major:** not critical, but may produce a product that does not comply with its authorization or specification, does not ensure effective implementation of required GMP controls, or combines several related other deficiencies into a systems failure.
**Other:** a departure from GMP that is neither critical nor major.

blocks.title: Training examples PIC/S lists as major deficiencies
blocks.text: Appendix 3 of PI 040-1 lists, among examples rated major in the absence of risk reducing factors: "Individuals in charge of QC/production not qualified by education, competency training and experience" and "Inadequate initial and ongoing training and/or no training records."

sections.heading: What should you do before the inspection?

items: Confirm every role entering production, storage, or quality control areas is in the training matrix, including maintenance, cleaning, and contractor staff.
Check that each training program is approved by the head of Production or Quality Control, as paragraph 2.11 requires.

Sample people in each area and trace them to training on the current procedure version, completed before they worked independently. [Version control for training content](/guides/how-to-maintain-version-control-for-training-content) makes this trace possible.
Gather effectiveness evidence, such as observed task performance, test results, or deviation trends, since paragraph 2.11 requires periodic assessment of practical effectiveness.
For sterile areas, confirm gowning qualifications are within the annual reassessment window.
Prepare a summary of personnel changes since the last inspection for the opening meeting.
Review open deviations and corrective actions that cite training, and close or explain them. See [using training in a CAPA](/guides/how-to-use-training-in-a-capa).

blocks.text: At the final meeting the inspector summarizes findings and discusses deficiencies and their importance so that deadlines for remedial action can be set. The EU procedure says facts and objective evidence should preferably be agreed with the company, which may discuss initial proposals for remedial action, and that the initial inspection report is sent to the company for comments so it can be finalized and, where applicable, a GMP certificate issued within the statutory 90 day timeframe.

A credible response to a training deficiency shows the root cause, retraining with effectiveness checks, changes to the training program or matrix, and an assessment of impact on product already made. The general method for assembling records is in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each GMP procedure version to the roles that use it, the training built from it, and each person's assessment evidence, so a site can show training on the current version and the effectiveness check Chapter 2 requires. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) and [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence).

faqs.q: Does EMA carry out GMP inspections itself?
faqs.a: GMP inspections in the EU are carried out by national competent authorities. EMA maintains the Compilation of Union Procedures on Inspections, which includes the procedure on conducting inspections of manufacturers and importers that inspectorates use, along with templates such as the Union format for GMP inspection reports.

faqs.q: Is a read and understood sign-off enough GMP training evidence?
faqs.a: Usually not by itself. Paragraph 2.11 requires the practical effectiveness of training to be periodically assessed, and PIC/S data integrity guidance expects evidence of training effectiveness on critical procedures. Pair sign-offs with observed performance or assessment for tasks that affect product quality.

faqs.q: Does the TGA follow the same rules as EU inspectors for training?
faqs.a: The TGA applies the PIC/S Guide to GMP through the manufacturing principles, and the Part I personnel paragraphs on training match EU GMP Chapter 2. The TGA adopts PE009-17 without Annexes 4, 5, and 14, and a separate Australian code applies to blood, tissues, and cellular therapy products.

faqs.q: Do cleaning and maintenance contractors need GMP training records?
faqs.a: Yes, if their duties take them into production or storage areas or control laboratories. Paragraph 2.10 extends training to technical, maintenance, and cleaning personnel and others whose activities could affect product quality, regardless of employment status.

factCheck.claim: EMA maintains compilation of inspection procedures used by EU/EEA GMP and GDP inspectorates; includes Conduct of inspections procedure.

Conduct of inspections procedure (adopted May 2023, in force 1 January 2024): prior announcement may be given; opening meeting normally no more than 30 minutes, company explains significant changes in personnel; 4.3 verbatim on discussing observations with key personnel, supervisors and operators to assess knowledge and competence; 4.5 general inspection includes Personnel; final meeting deficiencies discussed so deadlines fixed; facts preferably agreed; report sent for comments; GMP certificate within statutory 90-day timeframe; Union format of report.

PI 040-1 (entry into force 1 January 2019): purpose consistency and industry transparency; context and quality history; critical, major, other definitions; Appendix 3 major examples include individuals in charge of QC/production not qualified and inadequate initial and ongoing training and/or no training records.
PI 041-1 6.6.4: personnel qualified and trained for specific duties incl GdocPs; evidence of effectiveness of training on critical procedures such as electronic data review.
Chapter 2 paragraphs 2.7, 2.8, 2.10 to 2.14, 2.23; in operation 16 February 2014; Directive 2017/1572 Art 7(4) effectiveness verified (reused from EU GMP Chapter 2 page factCheck).
